en: Itivuttaka 62: Tikanipāta, Second Chapter Thus it was said by the Blessed One, so I have heard: “Monks, there are these three kinds of persons found existing in the world. What three? The person who is like a stone, the person who is like a water jar, and the person who is like a rain cloud. And how, monks, is one a person like a stone? Here, monks, a certain person dwells with his mind obsessed by sensual desire, and he does not understand as it really is: ‘My mind is obsessed by sensual desire. He dwells with his mind obsessed by ill will, and he does not understand as it really is: ‘My mind is obsessed by ill will. He dwells with his mind obsessed by dullness and drowsiness, and he does not understand as it really is: ‘My mind is obsessed by dullness and drowsiness. He dwells with his mind obsessed by restlessness and remorse, and he does not understand as it really is: ‘My mind is obsessed by restlessness and remorse. He dwells with his mind obsessed by doubt, and he does not understand as it really is: ‘My mind is obsessed by doubt. Just as a stone of great size, lying on the ground, would be struck by rain from a rain cloud, yet because of its hardness and weight, the water would not soak into it or penetrate deep within; even after many days and nights, that water would merely lie on the surface of the stone—so too, monks, is one a person like a stone. And how, monks, is one a person like a water jar? Here, monks, a certain person dwells with his mind obsessed by sensual desire, and he understands as it really is: ‘My mind is obsessed by sensual desire. He dwells with his mind obsessed by ill will... obsessed by dullness and drowsiness... obsessed by restlessness and remorse... obsessed by doubt, and he understands as it really is: ‘My mind is obsessed by doubt. Just as a water jar, full of water, placed on the ground, would be struck by rain from a rain cloud, and because it is full, the water would not soak into it or penetrate deep within; even after many days and nights, that water would merely lie on the surface of the jar—so too, monks, is one a person like a water jar. And how, monks, is one a person like a rain cloud? Here, monks, a certain person dwells with his mind obsessed by sensual desire, and he understands as it really is: ‘My mind is obsessed by sensual desire. He dwells with his mind obsessed by ill will... obsessed by dullness and drowsiness... obsessed by restlessness and remorse... obsessed by doubt, and he understands as it really is: ‘My mind is obsessed by doubt. Just as a rain cloud, having rained down, would cause the water to soak into the ground and penetrate deep within, and after many days and nights, that water would no longer be seen on the surface—so too, monks, is one a person like a rain cloud. These, monks, are the three kinds of persons found existing in the world. Thus spoke the Blessed One. Having said this, the Well-Farer rose from his seat and went to his dwelling. Then, not long after the Blessed One had departed, those monks addressed the Venerable Ānanda: “Friend Ānanda, it would be good if you were to explain in detail the meaning of what was stated in brief by the Blessed One. “Friends, as for what was stated in brief by the Blessed One, if I were to explain its meaning in detail, my head would split apart. However, the Blessed One has taught me this Dhamma discourse in such a way that I can explain it to you in detail. Listen, friends, and pay close attention; I shall speak. “Yes, friend,” those monks replied to the Venerable Ānanda. The Venerable Ānanda said this: “And how, friends, is one a person like a stone? Here, friends, a certain person dwells with his mind obsessed by sensual desire... ill will... dullness and drowsiness... restlessness and remorse... doubt, and he does not understand as it really is: ‘My mind is obsessed by doubt. Just as a stone of great size, lying on the ground, would be struck by rain from a rain cloud, yet because of its hardness and weight, the water would not soak into it or penetrate deep within; even after many days and nights, that water would merely lie on the surface of the stone—so too, friends, is one a person like a stone. And how, friends, is one a person like a water jar? Here, friends, a certain person dwells with his mind obsessed by sensual desire... ill will... dullness and drowsiness... restlessness and remorse... doubt, and he understands as it really is: ‘My mind is obsessed by doubt. Just as a water jar, full of water, placed on the ground, would be struck by rain from a rain cloud, and because it is full, the water would not soak into it or penetrate deep within; even after many days and nights, that water would merely lie on the surface of the jar—so too, friends, is one a person like a water jar. And how, friends, is one a person like a rain cloud? Here, friends, a certain person dwells with his mind obsessed by sensual desire... ill will... dullness and drowsiness... restlessness and remorse... doubt, and he understands as it really is: ‘My mind is obsessed by doubt. Just as a rain cloud, having rained down, would cause the water to soak into the ground and penetrate deep within, and after many days and nights, that water would no longer be seen on the surface—so too, friends, is one a person like a rain cloud. These, friends, are the three kinds of persons found existing in the world. This is what the Venerable Ānanda said. Having said this, the Teacher [the Blessed One] rose from his seat and entered his dwelling. Those monks were satisfied and delighted by the words of the Venerable Ānanda. Thus it was said by the Blessed One, so I have heard. This is the meaning of what was stated in brief by the Blessed One, and thus I have explained it in detail. May the Venerable Ones approve of my explanation. Thus it is approved by the Venerable Ones. Therefore, this is known as the "Discourse Spoken by the Teacher" (Sammukhābhāsasutta). The Discourse on the Faculties.
Thus it was said by the Blessed One, so I have heard:
"Bhikkhus, there are these three faculties."
Which three?
The faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown," the faculty of knowing,
and the faculty of one who has known— these, monks, are the three faculties.”
The Blessed One spoke this matter.
Regarding this, it is said:
“For one in training, who is still practicing the training...”
Following the straight path,
there is first the knowledge of destruction,
and immediately after that, full realization.
Then, for one liberated through final knowledge,
there arises the knowledge of such a one:
"My liberation is unshakable."
Through the destruction of the fetters of existence,
he is indeed endowed with the faculties,
peaceful, and delighting in the state of peace.
“He bears his final body, having conquered Māra and his host.
This matter was also spoken by the Blessed One; thus have I heard.
The third.
